newsitem.title: ITALY: Bildt sees long haul on "sick man" Serbia.
newsitem.headline: Bildt sees long haul on "sick man" Serbia.

text.p: Special envoy Carl Bildt said on Friday that Serbia was becoming the "sick man of Europe" with no way out of desperate economic straits unless President Slobodan Milosevic honoured opposition election victories.
Bildt, the international community's High Representative for Bosnia, painted a bleak picture of Serbia's future unless Milosevic agreed to democratic change.
He spoke at a news conference after a meeting in Rome of the multinational Contact Group on former Yugoslavia

He said the marathon political standoff over the Socialist government's annulment of municipal elections won by the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition last November was the "tip of the iceberg" in a far graver crisis.
"Serbia is in a desperate financial situation, (and) a desperate social situation," Bildt said.
"It is developing into the sick man of Europe and there is no way in which we can get the stability of Serbia and for the Serbs that we seek without fundamental economic reforms.
"Those are not going to be possible without an opening up to the outside world and the help that is there in the form of trade relations and financial relations," Bildt said.

"It's not something that even under the best of scenarios is going to be solved in one day, one week or one month. We will have to deal with the situation in Serbia and with Serbia for quite come time to come due to the depth of the crisis there."
Friday was the 76th consecutive day of street rallies across Serbia since the November 17 election outcome in 14 of the republic's 18 biggest cities was nullified.
A mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) led by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez has concluded that the balloting was fair.

The Contact Group, which comprises Bildt and senior officials of Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Russia, the United States and the Netherlands as European Union president, again called on Milosevic to honour the election results.
Italian diplomat Amadeo De Franchis, who chaired the meeting, said the Group had also appealed to both sides to refrain from violence.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum said Milosevic's failure to recognise the election results and engage in democratic dialogue was jeopardizing not only Serbia's future but also the prospects for all of former Yugoslavia.
"An isolated, undemocratic Serbia cannot contribute to peace in that region," Kornblum said.

"We cannot expect there to be the kind of open, prosperous and democratic future for the countries of former Yugoslavia that we all wish to have if Serbia remains an island of backwardness and undemocratic behaviour," he said.
